judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's arithmetic claims check out. (f o g)(3) = f(10) = 15 and (g o f)(3) = g(1) = 2, so the counterexample to commutativity is genuine; 3x + 7 = 22 gives 5; (f o g)(4) = f(-2) = -5 with the reversed order giving 7; 3((x-7)/3) + 7 simplifies to x; h(x) = (x-3)^2 on x >= 3 has inverse 3 + sqrt(x) so h^-1(16) = 7 while Sam's minus branch gives -1, outside the domain; x^2 = 9 gives plus/minus 3. The judge's claim about problem 8 is also supported - the model answer identifies sqrt(x^2) = |x|, names the skipped g(f(x)) direction, and states both domains. Where I part company is instruction_following 4/4. The worksheet's own directions say 'On the find-and-fix problems (4 and 6), name the mistake in one sentence and give the corrected value', and verify.json records both problems as pure eval entries with no manual companion. A named-error diagnosis recorded as machine-verified is the canonical case for manual flagging, and on a misconception-analysis sheet the diagnosis IS the learning objective.

strengths_to_preserve: Problems 1 and 2 make the student manufacture the non-commutativity counterexample themselves - (f o g)(3) = 15 against (g o f)(3) = 2 on the same pair - two problems before problem 4 asks them to diagnose Nia committing exactly that error. The sheet teaches the fact and then tests the diagnosis, in that order.

Both planted wrong values are declared as trap EXPRESSIONS - '(3*4 + 1) - 6' giving 7 and '3 - sqrt(16)' giving -1 - rather than typed numbers, so the key's 'Common wrong answers' block is computed from the misconception and cannot drift from it. This satisfies the prompt's 'declare any planted wrong results as machine-checked misconception traps' literally rather than nominally.

Problem 6 is the sharpest item on the sheet: h(x) = (x-3)^2 restricted to x >= 3, Sam's proposed h^-1(x) = 3 - sqrt(x) returning -1, and the test the stem asks for is whether -1 lies in the domain. The domain check IS the diagnosis rather than an afterthought, which is precisely the contracted focus.

The standards tag 'HSF-BF.A.1c, HSF-BF.B.4' is taken from references/standards-map.md line 97 ('Function composition/inverse') and matches the task contract exactly. Five other cases in this shard substituted a different code and justified it with a false claim about the map; this case shows the correct lookup is available, and it is worth preserving as the reference behaviour.

The study guide states the rule the whole sheet is built on - 'compose BOTH ways ... one direction alone can hide a domain restriction, so a single check is never a proof' - and problem 8 is then exactly a student who checked one direction.

root_causes.description: The two find-and-fix items, which are the reason this sheet exists, are recorded as pure numeric evals. The corrected VALUE is verified; the named-error sentence the worksheet directions explicitly require is not recorded at all, so the build reports one manual item where the instructional design has at least four.
evidence: Worksheet directions: 'On the find-and-fix problems (4 and 6), name the mistake in one sentence and give the corrected value.'
Problem 4: 'Explain in one sentence which composition Nia actually computed, then compute (f o g)(4) correctly'; verify.json id 4 is a single eval expecting -5.
Problem 6: 'Then state the correct inverse rule and compute h^-1(16)'; verify.json id 6 is a single eval expecting 7 - the inverse RULE, a second printed slot, is unrecorded.

Problems 2 ('state in one sentence what the comparison shows about the order of composition') and 7 ('explain in one sentence what your list proves about g having an inverse on all of R') are likewise eval-only.
gate_log.txt and final_response.md both report a single manual item, problem 8.

improvements.title: Any problem whose stem asks the student to explain, diagnose, name an error, or draw a representation must carry a manual verify entry
improvements.proposed_change: Add a rule to SKILL.md and a lint to the gate chain. Rule: a problem is machine-verified only for the quantities it computes; if its stem also carries an open-response imperative (explain, describe, justify, state why, say what/which/why, name the mistake, compare and state, plot, sketch, draw, label, complete the table) the verify JSON must carry an additional {"type": "manual"} entry under the same id describing what the written or drawn answer must contain. curr-334's verify.json in this same run is the working model - it pairs a machine entry per computed quantity with a manual entry per written diagnosis. Lint: scripts/verify.py already segments the worksheet .tex per problem for the prose-consistency gate; reuse that segmentation to scan each stem for the imperative list and fail when a matching problem has no manual entry.
improvements.regression_test: New fixture pairing curr-351's worksheet problem 4 stem ("Plot 3 + 4i. Then compute i(3+4i) ... and plot it too. Describe in one sentence what multiplying by i did to the arrow.") with a verify JSON holding only {"id": 4, "type": "eval", "expected": "-4 + 3*I"}. The lint must fail, naming problem 4 and the triggering words 'Plot' and 'Describe'. Today that exact pair builds green and reports '10 passed - 0 failed - 0 manual'.
improvements.expected_impact: Stops the delivered response claiming 'nothing on this sheet is open-ended' about sheets that are mostly open-ended, and restores the prompt's explicit requirement to label genuinely open responses for manual review. A grader currently receives a green build and no signal that half the sheet needs a human.
improvements.risk: Medium. A keyword scan over-fires on stems that say 'describe your method' as advice rather than as a graded slot, and on 'state the units' where the unit is already bound by answer_unit. Mitigate by keeping the imperative list short and explicit and by letting an author suppress a hit with an explicit "open_response": false marker on the problem, which is auditable.

improvements.title: One verify entry per printed response slot, including enumerated sub-parts and trailing second questions
improvements.proposed_change: Require the verify JSON to carry as many entries under an id as the printed problem has response slots. Sub-parts written as (a)/(b)/(c), and trailing extra questions ('Then check: what is m<A?', 'State how many zeros the theorem supplied'), each need their own entry - machine-typed where a value is computable, manual where it is not. Add a lint that, per problem segment of the worksheet .tex, counts enumerated \item sub-parts and \ansline / \answerline occurrences and fails when that count exceeds the number of verify entries sharing the id. curr-334 already satisfies this and should be cited in SKILL.md as the pattern to copy.
improvements.regression_test: New fixture from curr-301 problem 4: a stem enumerating (a) write the converse, (b) compute QR, (c) explain why PQRS makes the converse false, paired with the single verify entry {"id": 4, "type": "distance", "expected": 3}. The lint must fail with 'problem 4: 3 printed slots, 1 verify entry'. The current tree passes this fixture - it is what shipped.
improvements.expected_impact: Closes the largest verification blind spot in the shard: sheets that read as fully verified while a third of what the student writes is unrecorded, and answer keys whose Quick Answers bank prints one value for a two-answer question.
improvements.risk: Low-medium. The \item count is a heuristic: a sub-part that is pure scaffolding ('redraw the two triangles separately first') is not a response slot and would false-positive. Let the author mark such an item so the exclusion is auditable rather than silent.

case_summary: An excellent misconception-analysis sheet on composition order and inverse domains. All seven machine answers verify independently, both traps are machine-derived from the wrong method rather than typed, problem 6's restricted-domain inverse is a genuinely well-built diagnosis item, and the standards tag is correctly looked up from the map and matches the contract - worth noting because five sibling cases in this shard got that wrong. The one defect is that the find-and-fix items are recorded as pure numeric evals: the worksheet's own directions require a named-error sentence on problems 4 and 6, and problems 2 and 7 require a written conclusion, yet only problem 8 carries a manual entry. Nothing here is mathematically wrong and the ACCEPT stands, but a grader is told one item needs a human when four do.
